title: How God Saves Sinners and How We Know We Belong to Christ
content:
How God Saves Sinners and How We Know We Belong to Christ
The Disciple Code
How a Holy God Redeems Guilty Sinners Through Christ Alone
Romans 3:23 — “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 6:23 — “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Isaiah 53:5 — “He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities... and with his stripes we are healed.”
2 Corinthians 5:21 — “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Ephesians 2:8–9 — “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.”
John 3:16 — “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.”
1 John 5:13 — “These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life.”
The Greatest Question Every Person Must Answer
Every person will eventually wrestle with the same question, whether quietly in the depths of the heart or openly before others: How can I be made right with God? Wealth cannot answer it. Morality cannot satisfy it. Religion cannot remove it. The question remains because it is rooted in the very condition of mankind. Scripture never presents salvation as an improvement of an already good person, nor does it describe Christianity as simply adopting better habits. The gospel begins with the sobering reality that humanity stands guilty before a perfectly holy God, and unless He acts in mercy, no one can stand in His presence.
The apostle Paul removes every illusion of human righteousness when he writes, “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Earlier he concludes, “There is none righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10). These are not merely descriptions of particularly wicked people. They describe every descendant of Adam. Sin is not simply something we occasionally commit. It is the condition into which we are born. Every sinful thought, every selfish motive, every proud word, and every act of rebellion reveals what already exists within the human heart. Before the gospel can become good news, we must first understand why we need saving at all.
Our Greatest Problem Is Not Circumstances but Sin
The world often teaches that man’s greatest problems are found outside of himself. Scripture points somewhere entirely different. The deepest problem is not our upbringing, our failures, our enemies, or our circumstances. It is our separation from God because of sin. Isaiah declares, “Your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you” (Isaiah 59:2). Sin is not merely breaking a rule. It is rebellion against the holy Creator who made us for His glory.
Because God is perfectly just, He cannot overlook evil or pretend that sin does not matter. His holiness demands justice. Paul writes, “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 6:23). Death entered the world through sin, and apart from God’s intervention, eternal judgment is the righteous consequence of every sinner’s rebellion. This is why Scripture never presents salvation as something optional or merely beneficial. It is absolutely necessary, because without it every person remains under God’s righteous judgment.
The Cross Reveals Both God’s Justice and His Mercy
If God were only holy, every sinner would stand condemned without hope. If He were only loving while ignoring justice, He would cease to be righteous. The beauty of the gospel is that the cross satisfies both. At Calvary, God’s justice against sin was fully poured out, and His mercy toward sinners was fully displayed.
Centuries before Jesus was born, Isaiah foretold His sacrifice, writing, “He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities... and with his stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). Christ did not merely sympathize with sinners. He stood in their place. Paul explains the heart of the gospel in a single sentence: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Jesus lived the perfectly righteous life that no sinner could ever live, then willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved. Peter summarizes it simply: “For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
The resurrection declares that Christ’s sacrifice was accepted. Death could not hold Him because He was without sin, and His victory over the grave became the assurance that everyone united to Him by faith will also live. As Paul writes, Christ “was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification” (Romans 4:25). The empty tomb is God’s declaration that the work of redemption is complete.
Repentance and Faith Are the Biblical Response
When the gospel is preached, Scripture never calls people merely to become more religious or to improve their lives. It calls them to repent and believe. At the beginning of His public ministry Jesus proclaimed, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15). These two commands remain inseparable throughout the New Testament.
Repentance is often misunderstood as nothing more than feeling guilty or becoming emotional over sin. While sorrow for sin may accompany repentance, the Bible describes something much deeper. The Greek word metanoeō speaks of a change of mind that results in a changed direction. It is agreeing with God’s verdict about our sin, abandoning every false refuge, and turning toward Christ. Peter called the crowds to “Repent... for the remission of sins” (Acts 2:38), and later urged them, “Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19). Paul summarized his entire ministry as “repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21). Genuine repentance does not earn forgiveness. Rather, it is the posture of the heart that abandons self-rule and submits to the Lord who alone can save.
Faith is the companion of repentance. To repent is to turn from sin and self. To believe is to entrust yourself completely to Jesus Christ. Saving faith is not merely believing historical facts about His life, death, and resurrection. Even demons know those facts. Biblical faith rests entirely upon Christ’s finished work, acknowledging that there is nothing we can contribute to our salvation. Paul writes, “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). Salvation is received, never achieved.
Grace Leaves No Room for Human Boasting
From beginning to end, salvation belongs to the Lord. Left to ourselves, no one seeks God with a pure heart or possesses the righteousness necessary to enter His kingdom. Jesus Himself declared, “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44). The initiative always belongs to God.
This is why the gospel destroys every attempt to earn acceptance before Him. Good works are valuable, obedience matters deeply, and holy living is expected of every believer, but none of these things can remove guilt or satisfy divine justice. If righteousness could be earned, Christ would not have needed to die. Instead, God saves entirely by grace through the finished work of His Son. Every believer stands before Him clothed not in personal achievement but in the righteousness of Christ Himself. Grace humbles the proud because it reminds us that every part of salvation is a gift we could never deserve.
What Happens When God Saves a Sinner?
The moment a person trusts Christ, God does far more than forgive past sins. He makes that person new. Paul declares, “Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). Salvation is not merely receiving a second chance. It is receiving a new heart through the work of the Holy Spirit.
This new life begins to reshape every part of a believer’s affections. The Christian does not become sinless overnight, but neither does he remain unchanged. The desires that once ruled him begin to lose their mastery. Love for Christ grows. Love for God’s Word deepens. Conviction over sin becomes sharper because the Spirit now dwells within. Holiness is no longer viewed as a burden but as the joyful pursuit of knowing the One who first loved us.
The Evidence of Genuine Salvation
The New Testament repeatedly teaches that good works do not produce salvation, yet genuine salvation always produces fruit. Jesus taught that a tree is known by its fruit (Matthew 7:17–20). The fruit does not make the tree alive; it reveals the nature of the tree. In the same way, transformed lives reveal the reality of God’s transforming grace.
One of the clearest evidences is a growing love for Christ that expresses itself in obedience. Jesus said, “If ye love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). Obedience does not purchase God’s favor, nor is it perfect in this life, but it becomes the natural direction of a heart that has been changed by grace. John echoes this truth when he writes, “And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments” (1 John 2:3).
Another evidence is an ongoing pattern of repentance. Christians continue to battle sin, yet they no longer make peace with it. John writes, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8), but immediately reminds believers, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The believer’s life is marked not by sinless perfection but by continual dependence upon God’s mercy.
Scripture also points to love for fellow believers as evidence of spiritual life. “We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren” (1 John 3:14). This love is more than affection. It is the willingness to serve, forgive, encourage, and walk alongside those who belong to Christ because we recognize that we are members of the same family.
Paul further describes the Spirit’s work through the fruit He produces: “Love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance” (Galatians 5:22–23). These qualities are not manufactured through willpower alone. They grow because the Holy Spirit is actively conforming believers into the image of Christ. Growth is often gradual, sometimes difficult, but over time the direction of the believer’s life increasingly reflects the character of the Savior.
Can We Know That We Belong to Christ?
Many sincere believers struggle with assurance, wondering whether their faith is genuine. Scripture does not leave God’s children in constant uncertainty. The apostle John explains the purpose of his first letter with remarkable clarity: “These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).
Our confidence does not rest upon flawless obedience or perfect emotions. Feelings rise and fall, and even mature believers experience seasons of doubt. The foundation of assurance is God’s unchanging promise to all who trust His Son. Jesus declared, “He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life” (John 5:24). The evidences of salvation strengthen that assurance, but the ultimate ground of our confidence is the faithfulness of Christ, who promised never to cast out those who come to Him (John 6:37).
The Gospel Calls Every Sinner to Christ
The gospel is not an invitation for good people to become slightly better. It is God’s gracious call for guilty sinners to be reconciled to Him through His Son. Every person stands equally in need of mercy, and every person who comes to Christ in repentance and faith finds that His grace is sufficient. John writes, “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (John 3:16). Just two verses later he explains the dividing line between humanity: “He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already” (John 3:18).
This is the heart of the Christian faith. We are not saved because we have become worthy. We are saved because Christ is worthy. We are not accepted because of our righteousness, but because His righteousness has been credited to all who believe. The evidence of salvation is not a flawless life but a transformed one—a life that increasingly loves Christ, hates sin, delights in God’s Word, walks in repentance, bears the fruit of the Spirit, and perseveres because the Savior who began the work is faithful to complete it. In the end, every evidence points beyond itself to the One who accomplished our redemption. Salvation has always been, and will always be, the work of God from beginning to end.

title: The Table of Grace
content:
THE TABLE OF GRACE
THE DISCIPLE CODE
What Jesus Changed About Clean Foods,
Dietary Laws, and the New Covenant
Matthew 5:17 — "Don't misunderstand why I have come. I did not come to abolish the law of Moses or the writings of the prophets. No, I came to fulfill them.”
Mark 7:5 — “So the Pharisees and teachers of religious law asked him, "Why don't your disciples follow our age-old customs? For they eat without first performing the hand-washing ceremony."
Mark 7:15 — “You are not defiled by what you eat; you are defiled by what you say and do! "
1 Timothy 4:4 — “Since everything God created is good, we should not reject any of it. We may receive it gladly, with thankful hearts.”
The Question Is Bigger Than Bacon
Christians have argued about food for centuries. Can Christians eat pork? Did Jesus abolish the Old Testament dietary laws? If God called certain animals unclean in Leviticus, how can the New Testament call food clean? Did God change His mind, or are Christians simply ignoring commandments they no longer want to obey?
Those questions deserve more than a quick answer because they reach into something much larger than what belongs on a dinner plate. They force us to understand the purpose of God's Law, the distinction between the Old and New Covenants, the fulfillment accomplished by Jesus Christ, and what it actually means to live under the New Covenant.
Matthew 5:17 — "Don't misunderstand why I have come. I did not come to abolish the law of Moses or the writings of the prophets. No, I came to fulfill them.”
Jesus did not come to correct a mistake in the Law. He came to fulfill it.
God Called Israel to Be Different
The dietary laws begin with the holiness of God, not with nutrition.
Leviticus 11:44 — “After all, I, the LORD, am your God. You must be holy because I am holy. So do not defile yourselves by touching any of these animals that scurry along the ground.”
Israel belonged to the LORD, and its covenant life was intentionally different from the nations surrounding it. The distinction between clean and unclean animals was part of a much larger system involving sacrifices, priests, festivals, purification, circumcision, Sabbath observance, and the tabernacle.
These commands continually reminded Israel that the God dwelling among them was holy and that sinful humanity could not approach Him on its own terms.
Leviticus 11:46–47 — "These are the instructions regarding the land animals, the birds, and all the living things that move through the water or swarm over the earth,
so you can distinguish between what is unclean and may not be eaten and what is clean and may be eaten."
The dietary commands were therefore not meaningless restrictions that an ancient culture happened to adopt. God gave them within the Mosaic Covenant. They taught Israel to distinguish between clean and unclean, holy and common, and obedient and disobedient. God had separated Israel from the nations, and even ordinary activities such as eating reminded His people that they belonged to Him.
The Law Was Holy Because God Is Holy
Nothing about the New Covenant requires Christians to criticize the Old Covenant. Romans 7:12 — “But still, the law itself is holy and right and good.”
The Law was good because the God who gave it is good. The problem was never that God's commandments were defective. The problem was that sinful human beings could never achieve righteousness before God through their obedience to them.
The ceremonial system also taught through visible signs. Blood taught Israel that sin requires atonement. Priests demonstrated the need for mediation. Purification demonstrated the reality of uncleanness. The tabernacle demonstrated that access to God's presence could occur only according to God's command. Clean and unclean foods belonged within that same covenantal world. Each distinction pointed beyond ordinary life toward the holiness of the God who had redeemed Israel.
By the Time of Jesus, Food Was Part of Identity
By the first century, dietary practices had become deeply woven into Jewish identity. Israel had lived through conquest, exile, foreign occupation, and enormous cultural pressure. Circumcision, Sabbath observance, and dietary practices visibly distinguished faithful Jews from their Gentile neighbors. What a person ate, how food was prepared, and with whom someone shared a table could carry enormous religious and social significance.
Mark 7:5 “So the Pharisees and teachers of religious law asked him, "Why don't your disciples follow our age-old customs? For they eat without first performing the hand-washing ceremony."
The controversy begins because Jesus' disciples were eating without performing the ceremonial handwashing expected by the Pharisees and teachers of religious law.
The immediate controversy is therefore not simply whether someone can eat pork. It concerns ritual purity and what Mark calls the tradition of the elders.
Jesus Went Straight After the Heart
Jesus refused to allow human tradition to carry the authority of God's Word.
Mark 7:8 — “For you ignore God's specific laws and substitute your own traditions."
The Pharisees had become intensely concerned with outward contamination, but Jesus moved the discussion from hands, dishes, and food directly into the human heart.
Mark 7:15 — “You are not defiled by what you eat; you are defiled by what you say and do! "
Then Jesus identifies what actually defiles a person.
Mark 7:21–23 — “For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness.
All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person."
Sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, lust, envy, slander, pride, and foolishness do not originate in the stomach. They come from within. The deepest human problem has never been contaminated food. It is a contaminated heart.
This prepares the reader for one of the most important statements in the entire discussion.
MARK 7:19
What Does** ***Katharizōn*** **Actually Mean?
At the conclusion of Jesus' explanation, the Greek text contains the phrase:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
katharizōn panta ta brōmata
The word *katharizōn comes from katharizō, carrying the sense of cleansing, making clean, or purifying*. The disagreement surrounding this verse is sometimes described as though the King James Version and modern translations were translated from completely different Greek words. That description is misleading. The major issue is how the Greek construction should be understood grammatically.
The KJV renders:
Mark 7:19 — “Food doesn't come in contact with your heart, but only passes through the stomach and then comes out again." (By saying this, he showed that every kind of food is acceptable.)”
Many modern translations communicate the construction as Mark's explanatory conclusion: Jesus declared all foods clean.
This is a translation question, not a different Bible
Ancient Greek manuscripts did not contain modern English quotation marks, parentheses, commas, and other punctuation exactly as they appear in contemporary Bibles. Translators therefore must determine how clauses relate grammatically to one another.
The form *katharizōn* is particularly important because it is a masculine nominative participle. This grammatical construction contributes to the understanding found in many modern translations that the phrase functions as an explanatory comment concerning what Jesus had just said rather than merely describing the digestive system physically purging food.
The important point is that modern translations did not simply invent the statement because translators wanted Christians to eat previously forbidden foods. The rendering comes from an attempt to understand the Greek syntax.
But Christianity does not have to rest the entire case upon one Greek participle.
The rest of the New Testament makes the direction unmistakable.
The Table of Grace
Colossians 2:17 — “Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.”
There is a relationship between the covenants. A shadow is real, and it points beyond itself. The sacrifices were shadows. The priesthood was a shadow. The tabernacle was a shadow. Ceremonial purification was a shadow. These things taught genuine truths about God, holiness, sin, atonement, and cleansing, but they were never the final destination.
Hebrews 10:1 — “For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.”
Jesus is the substance toward which those shadows pointed.
When Christ arrived, God did not become less holy. Instead, everything represented through the ceremonial system reached its fulfillment in Him. The question therefore is not whether Christians decided to abandon Moses. The question is what happens to the Mosaic ceremonial system when the Messiah to whom it pointed finally comes.
ACTS 10
Peter Had to Learn It Too
Peter had walked with Jesus, witnessed the resurrection, and received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, yet the categories of clean and unclean food remained deeply embedded within him.
Then came the vision.
Acts 10:13 — “And there came a voice to him, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat”
Peter immediately resisted.
Acts 10:14 — “But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.”
The response came:
Acts 10:15 — “And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.”
The command was repeated three times.
Acts 10:16 – “This was done thrice: and the vessel was received up again into heaven.”
Acts 10 is about more than Peter's diet. Immediately afterward, Gentile messengers sent by Cornelius arrived. Peter eventually understood the larger significance.
Acts 10:28 — “And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.””
Food imagery was being used within a much larger revelation: Peter must no longer regard Gentiles as inherently unclean people from whom God's covenant blessing must be withheld.
The Table Was Opening to the Nations
The early church suddenly faced a situation almost unimaginable to previous generations. Jewish believers and Gentile believers were now brothers in the same Messiah. They worshiped the same Lord, received the same Spirit, and were being brought into the same people of God.
Acts 10:34–35 — “So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality,
but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.”
This created enormous practical questions. Must Gentiles become Jews before becoming Christians? Must they be circumcised? Must they observe Israel's dietary laws? Must they adopt the Mosaic ceremonial system?
Acts 15 would confront those questions directly.
The Gospel was going to the nations, and Gentiles were not required to become ethnic Israelites before they could belong to Jesus Christ.
ROMANS 14
Nothing is unclean in itself
Romans 14:14 — “I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean.”
Romans 14:20 — “Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats.”
The New Testament does not treat food as possessing inherent spiritual uncleanness. Yet Romans 14 immediately prevents Christian liberty from becoming selfishness. A believer may possess the freedom to eat something while voluntarily choosing not to exercise that freedom around another believer whose conscience would be seriously troubled.
This is not surrendering the Gospel but rather it is practicing love.
Christian Liberty Is Not Permission to Become Selfish
Christian liberty means that where God has not bound the conscience, another person does not possess the authority to invent a commandment and bind it for Him. At the same time, Christian liberty never means that personal freedom is more important than another believer.
Romans 14:15 — “For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.”
The mature Christian does not ask only, “Am I allowed to do this?”, he also asks whether exercising that freedom is wise, loving, edifying, and honoring to Christ.
There is a tremendous difference between voluntarily abstaining from a food and teaching that abstaining from that food makes someone righteous before God.
1 TIMOTHY 4
God's Creation Is Still Good
1 Timothy 4:1-2 — “Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,”
Certain teachers were forbidding things God had created to be received with thanksgiving. The response reaches back toward creation itself.
1 Timothy 4:3-4 — “who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving,”
Christianity does not teach that physical creation is inherently evil. God created the world and called His creation good. Food does not possess the ability to spiritually contaminate a Christian merely because of its material composition.
The New Covenant emphasis therefore moves toward receiving God's provision with gratitude while living under the authority of His Word.
COLOSSIANS 2
Don't Let Someone Judge Your Salvation by Your Plate
Colossians 2:16 — “So don't let anyone condemn you for what you eat or drink, or for not celebrating certain holy days or new-moon ceremonies or Sabbaths.”
Food. Drink. Festivals. New moons. Sabbaths.
Then comes the reason:
Colossians 2:17 — “For these rules were only shadows of the real thing, Christ himself.”
The substance is Christ.
This is where dietary discussions can become spiritually dangerous. A Christian may choose not to eat pork. Another may follow dietary practices resembling those found in Leviticus. Someone may abstain for health, conscience, culture, or personal discipline.
Nothing about Christian liberty requires a believer to eat every permissible food.
The problem begins when personal abstinence becomes a condition of righteousness before God or a standard by which the salvation of another believer is judged.
DID GOD CHANGE HIS MIND?
No. Christ Fulfilled What the Law Anticipated.
The Old and New Testaments are not competing religions. They tell one unfolding story of redemption.
The Mosaic Covenant was genuinely given by God to Israel. Its sacrifices, priesthood, ceremonies, purity regulations, festivals, and dietary distinctions belonged within God's redemptive purpose.
Then Christ came.
Matthew 5:17 — "Don't misunderstand why I have come. I did not come to abolish the law of Moses or the writings of the prophets. No, I came to fulfill them.”
Fulfillment is not contradiction.
A promise is not contradicted when it is fulfilled. A shadow is not rejected when the substance arrives. A signpost has not failed when the traveler finally reaches the destination toward which it was pointing.
Jesus stands at the center of the entire transition.
The Law Could Identify Uncleanness. It Could Not Clean the Heart.
This is where the entire discussion returns to Mark 7.
The great human problem was never pork.
It was sin.
A man could carefully avoid every ceremonially unclean animal and still possess a heart filled with pride, lust, greed, deceit, hatred, and unbelief.
Mark 7:21 — “Not all people who sound religious are really godly. They may refer to me as 'Lord,' but they still won't enter the Kingdom of Heaven. The decisive issue is whether they obey my Father in heaven.”
Ceremonial cleanliness could teach the necessity of holiness, but it could never create holiness within the human heart. Only Christ can do that.
Hebrews 9:14 — “Just think how much more the blood of Christ will purify our hearts from deeds that lead to death so that we can worship the living God. For by the power of the eternal Spirit, Christ offered himself to God as a perfect sacrifice for our sins.”
The cleansing humanity ultimately needed could never come from changing the menu.
It required blood. The blood of Jesus Christ.
The Cross changes the entire question
At the cross, Jesus did what ceremonial regulations could only anticipate. He bore the guilt of His people, satisfied divine justice, and provided the cleansing sinners actually needed.
1 Peter 2:24 — “He personally carried away our sins in his own body on the cross so we can be dead to sin and live for what is right. You have been healed by his wounds!”
The Christian therefore does not stand before God declared righteous because he successfully maintained Israel's dietary distinctions.
He stands righteous because he belongs to Christ.
His confidence is not his plate.
His confidence is the cross.
What Should a Christian Do Today?
Receive God's provision with thanksgiving.
1 Timothy 4:4 — “Since everything God created is good, we should not reject any of it. We may receive it gladly, with thankful hearts.”
Never use freedom as an excuse for sin or selfishness.
Romans 14:15 — “And if another Christian is distressed by what you eat, you are not acting in love if you eat it. Don't let your eating ruin someone for whom Christ died.”
Never condemn a brother over food where Christ has granted liberty.
Colossians 2:16 — “So don't let anyone condemn you for what you eat or drink, or for not celebrating certain holy days or new-moon ceremonies or Sabbaths.”
Never confuse personal discipline with justification.
Romans 5:1 — “Therefore, since we have been made right in God's sight by faith, we have peace with God because of what Jesus Christ our Lord has done for us.”
And never forget what the dietary laws were ultimately teaching: God is holy, mankind is unclean, and we desperately need cleansing that we cannot provide for ourselves.
THE TABLE OF GRACE
The dietary laws were never meaningless. They belonged to God's covenant with Israel and taught generations of His people about holiness, separation, purity, obedience, and the seriousness of approaching a holy God.
But they were never the Savior.
The Law could tell a man that something was unclean. It could not give him a clean heart.
The priest could pronounce someone ceremonially clean. He could not justify a sinner before the judgment seat of God.
The sacrifice could point toward atonement. It could not finally remove sin.
The Table was waiting for its fulfillment.
The fulfillment is Jesus Christ.
Our righteousness does not come from what we refuse to eat.
Our righteousness comes from Christ.
Our cleansing does not begin in the stomach.
It begins with the blood of Christ cleansing sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
The Christian can therefore receive God's creation with thanksgiving, exercise his liberty with love, respect the conscience of his brother, refuse the chains of legalism, and pursue genuine holiness with his eyes fixed upon Jesus.
Christ is the substance.

title: Prayer
content:
Prayer
The Disciple Code
Hebrews 4:14–16 (NLT)
" That is why we have a great High Priest who has gone to heaven, Jesus the Son of God. Let us cling to him and never stop trusting him.
This High Priest of ours understands our weaknesses, for he faced all of the same temptations we do, yet he did not sin.
So let us come boldly to the throne of our gracious God. There we will receive his mercy, and we will find grace to help us when we need it.”
Matthew 6:5–8 (NLT)
"And now about prayer. When you pray, don't be like the hypocrites who love to pray publicly on street corners and in the synagogues where everyone can see them. I assure you, that is all the reward they will ever get.
But when you pray, go away by yourself, shut the door behind you, and pray to your Father secretly. Then your Father, who knows all secrets, will reward you.
"When you pray, don't babble on and on as people of other religions do. They think their prayers are answered only by repeating their words again and again.
Don't be like them, because your Father knows exactly what you need even before you ask him!”
Luke 11:1–4 (NLT)
" Once when Jesus had been out praying, one of his disciples came to him as he finished and said, "Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples."
He said, "This is how you should pray: "Father, may your name be honored. May your Kingdom come soon.
Give us our food day by day.
And forgive us our sins--just as we forgive those who have sinned against us. And don't let us yield to temptation. "
John 14:6 (NLT)
" Jesus told him, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one can come to the Father except through me.
Ephesians 2:18 (NLT)
" Now all of us, both Jews and Gentiles, may come to the Father through the same Holy Spirit because of what Christ has done for us.
Why Did God Give Us Prayer?
Every believer eventually comes to the same question. If God already knows everything, why would He command His children to pray? Jesus answered that question before anyone asked it.
"When you pray, don't babble on and on as people of other religions do. They think their prayers are answered only by repeating their words again and again.
Don't be like them, because your Father knows exactly what you need even before you ask him!” Matthew 6:7–8,
He warned His disciples not to imitate those who believed that God could be persuaded through endless repetition or impressive words. Then He reminded them that "your Father knows exactly what you need even before you ask him." God is never learning something new when we pray.
He already knows every burden we carry, every temptation we face, every fear we hide, and every need we have. Prayer, therefore, cannot exist because God lacks information. It exists because God desires relationship with His children.
From the beginning of the Bible, it reveals that God's desire has always been to dwell with His people. Sin shattered that fellowship, separating mankind from a holy God and leaving us unable to approach Him on our own. The entire Old Testament points forward to the One who would restore what had been lost.
" That is why we have a great High Priest who has gone to heaven, Jesus the Son of God. Let us cling to him and never stop trusting him.
This High Priest of ours understands our weaknesses, for he faced all of the same temptations we do, yet he did not sin.
So let us come boldly to the throne of our gracious God. There we will receive his mercy, and we will find grace to help us when we need it.” Hebrews 4:14–16 is a great invitation.
Jesus Christ is our great High Priest who has entered heaven on our behalf, and because of His finished work we are invited to come boldly before God's throne of grace. We do not approach Him because we have earned another audience with heaven or because we have lived faithfully enough to deserve His attention. We come because Jesus has opened the way through His death and resurrection. Prayer is not the reward for mature Christians. It is the privilege of every believer who has been redeemed by Christ.
This truth also reshapes the purpose of prayer. Many people approach prayer hoping to convince God to change His mind or persuade Him to accomplish their plans. Jesus teaches something altogether different. Prayer is God's appointed means of drawing us into deeper dependence upon Him.
Philippians 4:6–7, “Don't worry about anything; instead, pray about everything. Tell God what you need, and thank him for all he has done. If you do this, you will experience God's peace, which is far more wonderful than the human mind can understand. His peace will guard your hearts and minds as you live in Christ Jesus.”
He does not promise that every hardship will disappear immediately. Instead, he promises that God's peace will guard our hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. Often, before God changes our circumstances, He changes the man who is praying. Anxiety begins to give way to trust. Pride is replaced with humility. Fear slowly yields to faith. The heart that once tried to control every outcome gradually learns to rest in the wisdom of God.
“So humble yourselves under the mighty power of God, and in his good time he will honor you. Give all your worries and cares to God, for he cares about what happens to you.” 1 Peter 5:6–7, urging us as believers to humble ourselves under God's mighty hand and cast every care upon Him because He cares for them. Prayer is one of the clearest expressions of humility found anywhere in Scripture. Every sincere prayer acknowledges that we are not self-sufficient. It confesses that our wisdom is limited, our strength is insufficient, and our hope rests entirely upon the Lord.
The strongest man is not the one who never asks for help. The strongest man is the one who continually brings every burden to the feet of Jesus, trusting that his heavenly Father knows him completely, loves him perfectly, and will always do what is best according to His perfect will.
Prayer is far more than asking God for things. It is the daily privilege of walking with the Father through the Son by the power of the Holy Spirit. Every time we pray, we are reminded that God has not merely answered our greatest need by forgiving our sins through Christ. He has also invited us into a relationship that will continue throughout this life and into eternity. That is why prayer has never been about informing God. It has always been about knowing Him.
How Did Jesus Pray?
If we truly want to understand prayer, there is no greater teacher than Jesus Christ. Throughout the Gospels, the disciples witnessed Him teaching with authority, calming storms, healing the sick, raising the dead, and confronting religious leaders with perfect wisdom. Yet the only recorded occasion where they specifically asked Him to teach them something was when they observed His prayer life.
“Once when Jesus had been out praying, one of his disciples came to him as he finished and said, "Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples." Luke 11:1, after watching Jesus pray, they simply said, "Lord, teach us to pray." They had seen something different. His prayers were not empty religious exercises or routine traditions. They were the natural expression of His perfect fellowship with the Father. The disciples recognized that everything Jesus did flowed from that relationship, and they longed to understand it for themselves.
In Jesus' prayer life is that He intentionally made time to be alone with His Father. “The next morning Jesus awoke long before daybreak and went out alone into the wilderness to pray.” Mark 1:35 says, before daybreak while everyone else was still asleep, Jesus withdrew to a solitary place to pray. The previous day had been filled with teaching, healing, and ministering to countless people, yet before another demand was allowed to shape His day, He sought communion with the Father.
Jesus prayed before making significant decisions. “One day soon afterward Jesus went to a mountain to pray, and he prayed to God all night.” Luke 6:12–13.
Before choosing the twelve apostles who would carry the Gospel into the world, Jesus spent the entire night in prayer. He did not rely upon human instinct, popularity, or outward appearances. Although He possessed perfect wisdom, He demonstrated complete dependence upon His Father. For believers today, this example reminds us that prayer is not simply reserved for emergencies. The decisions that shape our families, our ministries, our careers, and our future should first be placed before God. A man who consistently seeks the Lord before making important decisions is acknowledging that God's wisdom far exceeds his own.
“Then, accompanied by the disciples, Jesus left the upstairs room and went as usual to the Mount of Olives.
There he told them, "Pray that you will not be overcome by temptation."
He walked away, about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed,
"Father, if you are willing, please take this cup of suffering away from me. Yet I want your will, not mine."
Then an angel from heaven appeared and strengthened him.
He prayed more fervently, and he was in such agony of spirit that his sweat fell to the ground like great drops of blood.
At last he stood up again and returned to the disciples, only to find them asleep, exhausted from grief.
"Why are you sleeping?" he asked. "Get up and pray. Otherwise temptation will overpower you." Luke 22:39–46.
Knowing that the cross was only hours away, Jesus poured out His heart before the Father. He did not hide His anguish or pretend that suffering would be easy. He honestly expressed the weight of what lay before Him, yet His prayer concluded with complete surrender: "Yet I want your will to be done, not mine." These words teach one of the greatest lessons in all of Scripture. Faithful prayer is not measured by whether we receive everything we ask for. Faithful prayer is measured by whether we trust God enough to submit to His will even when His answer leads us through suffering instead of around it. Jesus teaches us that true prayer is not an attempt to bend God's will toward ours but a willingness to surrender our lives to His perfect wisdom.
What Makes a Biblical Prayer?
When the disciples asked Jesus to teach them how to pray, He did not hand them a script to memorize. Instead, He gave them a pattern that would shape the way they thought about God, themselves, and the purpose of prayer.
Jesus said Pray like this: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be honored.
May your Kingdom come soon. May your will be done here on earth, just as it is in heaven. Give us our food for today, and forgive us our sins, just as we have forgiven those who have sinned against us. And don't let us yield to temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. Matthew 6:9–13.
Those words remind us that the Lord's Prayer is not simply something to repeat without thought. It is a model that teaches us what matters most to God. Every phrase moves our attention away from ourselves and toward our heavenly Father before we ever begin presenting our own requests. Jesus is not teaching us to become experts at saying the right words. He is teaching us to become men whose hearts have been shaped by the right priorities.
Jesus begins with the words, "Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy." Before we ask for daily bread, guidance, or protection, we are reminded of who God is. Prayer begins with worship because worship puts everything else into its proper perspective. It reminds us that the One we are approaching is not merely stronger than we are, but infinitely holy, perfectly wise, and completely trustworthy. Many of our prayers become anxious because we begin with our problems instead of beginning with God. When our first concern is His holiness, His greatness, and His glory, our fears begin to shrink in light of His greatness. A man who spends time worshipping before asking will often discover that his greatest need is not changed circumstances but a greater view of God.
Jesus immediately continues by saying, "May your Kingdom come soon. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven." These words challenge one of the greatest misconceptions about prayer. Prayer is not an attempt to convince God to support our plans. It is the daily surrender of our lives to His plans. Every believer naturally wants God to bless his family, his work, and his future, but Jesus teaches us to ask an even greater question: "Lord, what are You accomplishing, and how can my life be used for Your glory?" A biblical prayer is not centered on building our own kingdom. It is centered on advancing God's kingdom. As our love for Christ grows, our prayers gradually become less focused on comfort and increasingly focused on faithfulness.
Only after establishing God's glory and God's will does Jesus teach us to pray, "Give us today the food we need." This simple request reminds us that God genuinely cares about the ordinary details of life. He is not only concerned with great spiritual victories but also with the daily needs of His children. Scripture never portrays dependence as weakness. Instead, dependence is one of the defining characteristics of biblical faith. Every meal, every opportunity to work, every breath we take, and every blessing we enjoy ultimately comes from the gracious hand of God. Prayer continually reminds us that we are receivers before we are achievers. Everything we possess is a gift of God's grace.
Jesus then turns our attention toward confession by saying, "Forgive us our sins, as we have forgiven those who sin against us." Healthy prayer always includes honest repentance. The Christian who regularly spends time in God's presence becomes increasingly aware of his need for grace. Confession is not an attempt to earn forgiveness, because Christ has already paid for the sins of His people on the cross. Rather, confession restores fellowship with our Father and keeps our hearts tender before Him. At the same time, Jesus connects receiving forgiveness with extending forgiveness. A heart that continually remembers the mercy of God will increasingly become a heart that offers mercy to others. Bitterness, resentment, and unforgiveness cannot thrive where the Gospel is treasured.
Finally, Jesus teaches us to pray, "Don't let us yield to temptation, but rescue us from the evil one." The Christian life is a spiritual battle, and Jesus never tells His followers to face that battle alone. Every day we are confronted with temptations that appeal to our flesh, challenge our convictions, and seek to draw us away from Christ. Prayer reminds us that victory over sin is never accomplished through self-confidence but through daily dependence upon God. We ask for wisdom because we know our own understanding is limited. We ask for strength because we know our own strength will eventually fail. We ask for protection because we recognize that apart from God's sustaining grace, we are vulnerable to temptation.
A biblical prayer is not measured by its length, its emotion, or its eloquence. It is measured by whether it reflects the heart of God. The man who prays biblically worships before he asks, submits before he demands, trusts before he worries, confesses before he excuses, forgives because he has been forgiven, and depends upon God rather than himself. As Jesus teaches His disciples, prayer is not simply about learning to speak to God. It is about learning to think like a citizen of His kingdom.
"The Lord is close to all who call on him, yes, to all who call on him in truth." Psalm 145:18.
God is not searching for polished speeches or perfect language. He delights in hearts that come before Him with sincerity, humility, faith, and love.
Jesus promises “But if you stay joined to me and my words remain in you, you may ask any request you like, and it will be granted!” John 15:7, that as we remain in Him and His words remain in us, our desires begin to align with His will. The closer we walk with Christ through His Word, the more our prayers begin to reflect His heart.
Paul encourages in Colossians 4:2 “Devote yourselves to prayer with an alert mind and a thankful heart.”  A life devoted to prayer is ultimately a life devoted to knowing God Himself, and there is no greater privilege that has been given to those who belong to Jesus Christ.
Why Doesn't God Always Answer the Way We Want?
One of the greatest struggles we face is not learning how to pray but learning how to trust God when His answer is different than the one we hoped to receive. Nearly every Christian has experienced seasons where prayers seemed to go unanswered. A loved one was not healed. A marriage was not restored. A job opportunity never came. A burden remained longer than expected. During those moments, it is easy to wonder whether God is listening at all. The Bible does not ignore those questions. Instead, it answers them by continually directing our attention back to the character of God rather than to our circumstances. Scripture never promises that God will answer every request exactly as we desire, but it repeatedly assures us that He is always faithful, always wise, and always working for His glory and the good of those who love Him.
“You want what you don't have, so you scheme and kill to get it. You are jealous for what others have, and you can't possess it, so you fight and quarrel to take it away from them. And yet the reason you don't have what you want is that you don't ask God for it.
And even when you do ask, you don't get it because your whole motive is wrong--you want only what will give you pleasure.” James 4:2–3.
Some believers ask with motives that are centered on themselves rather than on God's purposes. Prayer is never intended to become a means of convincing God to satisfy our selfish ambitions. The Lord loves His children too much to give them everything they desire if those desires would ultimately draw them away from Him. Just as a loving father sometimes refuses a request because he sees dangers his child cannot yet understand, our heavenly Father often withholds what we ask because He sees the entire picture while we see only a single moment. His refusals are not evidence of indifference but expressions of His perfect wisdom.
“even though I have received wonderful revelations from God. But to keep me from getting puffed up, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger from Satan to torment me and keep me from getting proud.
Three different times I begged the Lord to take it away.
Each time he said, "My gracious favor is all you need. My power works best in your weakness." So now I am glad to boast about my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may work through me.
Since I know it is all for Christ's good, I am quite content with my weaknesses and with insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.” 2 Corinthians 12:7–10.
Paul pleaded with the Lord three different times to remove what he described as a thorn in the flesh. We are never told exactly what that thorn was, but we are told God's answer. The Lord did not remove the trial. Instead, He said, "My grace is all you need. My power works best in weakness." Paul discovered that the greatest answer to his prayer was not the removal of suffering but the presence of Christ in the midst of it. Sometimes God demonstrates His power by changing our circumstances. At other times He demonstrates His power by sustaining us through them. Both are expressions of His grace.
What Hinders Prayer?
Every Christian has experienced seasons when prayer feels difficult. Sometimes we pray and immediately sense God's peace. Other times heaven seems silent, and we begin asking whether God is listening at all. The Bible never teaches that God abandons His children or stops loving them. Through Jesus Christ, believers have been permanently accepted into God's family. However, Scripture does teach that there are attitudes and patterns of life that hinder our fellowship with God and weaken our prayer life. The issue is not that God has become distant from His children, but that we often allow sin, pride, or unbelief to create barriers in our own hearts. The same God who invites us to pray also lovingly reveals the things that keep us from enjoying close fellowship with Him.
David understood this reality when he wrote in Psalms 66:18, "If I had not confessed the sin in my heart, the Lord would not have listened." David is not teaching that believers lose their salvation every time they sin. Rather, he is describing the reality that cherished, unrepentant sin disrupts our fellowship with God. Every healthy relationship requires honesty, and our relationship with the Lord is no different. When we knowingly excuse sin, justify disobedience, or refuse to repent, we should not expect to enjoy intimate communion with the God whose very nature is holy. Confession does not earn God's forgiveness, because forgiveness was purchased through the cross of Christ. Confession restores fellowship by bringing our hearts back into the light of God's grace.
Isaiah 59:1–2, “Listen! The LORD is not too weak to save you, and he is not becoming deaf. He can hear you when you call.
But there is a problem--your sins have cut you off from God. Because of your sin, he has turned away and will not listen anymore.”
God's power had not diminished and His ears had not become deaf. The problem was not God's ability to hear but the people's unwillingness to turn from their rebellion. Their sin had created a barrier between them and the God they claimed to worship. While Isaiah was speaking specifically to the nation of Israel under the Old Covenant, the principle remains instructive for every believer. Sin always damages fellowship. Every time we tolerate what God calls us to forsake, we weaken our sensitivity to His voice. The answer is never to hide from God in shame but to return to Him in repentance, trusting the mercy that has already been secured through Jesus Christ.
1 Peter 3:7, “In the same way, you husbands must give honor to your wives. Treat her with understanding as you live together. She may be weaker than you are, but she is your equal partner in God's gift of new life. If you don't treat her as you should, your prayers will not be heard.”
Peter addresses husbands directly. He instructs them to honor their wives with understanding so that their prayers will not be hindered. This verse reminds us that our relationship with God cannot be separated from the way we treat the people He has entrusted to us. A man cannot consistently neglect, dishonor, or wound those around him while expecting rich fellowship with the Lord. Genuine spirituality is never measured only by private devotion. It is revealed by daily obedience. The man who walks closely with God will increasingly reflect the character of Christ within his marriage, his family, his workplace, and his church.
Every obstacle to prayer ultimately points us back to the Gospel. Pride is overcome through humility before the cross. Unconfessed sin is met with forgiveness through Christ. Doubt is answered by the faithfulness of God's promises. Selfish ambition is transformed as we seek first His kingdom. Broken relationships are restored as we extend the same grace we have received. None of these changes happen through human determination alone. They are the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit in the life of a man who continually returns to Christ. The greatest hindrance to prayer is not that God has become unwilling to listen. It is that we often drift from the very fellowship He has graciously invited us to enjoy. The answer has always been the same: return to Jesus, remain in His Word, and walk daily with the Father who delights in hearing the prayers of His children.
Becoming a Man of Prayer
1 Thessalonians 5:16–18 (NLT) — “Always be joyful. Keep on praying. No matter what happens, always be thankful, for this is God's will for you who belong to Christ Jesus.”
Colossians 4:2 (NLT) — “Devote yourselves to prayer with an alert mind and a thankful heart.”
Psalms 5:1–3 (NLT) — “Have mercy on me, O God, because of your unfailing love. Because of your great compassion, blot out the stain of my sins.
Wash me clean from my guilt. Purify me from my sin.
For I recognize my shameful deeds--they haunt me day and night.”
Ephesians 6:18 (NLT) — “Pray at all times and on every occasion in the power of the Holy Spirit. Stay alert and be persistent in your prayers for all Christians everywhere.”
Matthew 26:41 (NLT) — “Keep alert and pray. Otherwise temptation will overpower you. For though the spirit is willing enough, the body is weak!"
Every man wants a stronger prayer life, but many never develop one because they are waiting for the perfect moment. They assume that one day life will slow down, distractions will disappear, and they will finally have enough time to consistently meet with God. The Bible presents a very different picture. The men who walked closely with God were not those who happened to have fewer responsibilities. They were men who chose to make fellowship with God their highest priority. Prayer was not something they squeezed into the empty spaces of life. It became the foundation upon which everything else was built. A healthy prayer life is not created by finding more time. It is created by deciding that time with God is worth protecting above almost everything else.
1 Thessalonians 5:16–18, "Always be joyful. Never stop praying. Be thankful in all circumstances, for this is God's will for you who belong to Christ Jesus."
At first glance, those words seem impossible. Surely Paul is not suggesting that believers spend every waking moment with their heads bowed and their eyes closed. Instead, he is describing a life that remains continually aware of God's presence. Prayer is no longer reserved for church services, family meals, or moments of crisis. It becomes the ongoing conversation of a heart that is walking with its Father. Throughout the day, decisions become opportunities to seek wisdom, blessings become opportunities for thanksgiving, temptations become opportunities to ask for strength, and burdens become opportunities to trust the Lord rather than carrying them alone.
This kind of prayer life is built through intentional habits.
David writes in Psalm 5:1–3, "Listen to my voice in the morning, Lord. Each morning I bring my requests to you and wait expectantly."
Before the responsibilities of the day competed for his attention, David sought the Lord. There is nothing in Scripture that commands every believer to pray at sunrise, yet there is tremendous wisdom in beginning each day with God before the world begins speaking into our minds. The first voices we hear each morning often shape the direction of the rest of the day. If we begin with news, social media, work, or endless distractions, those voices frequently dominate our thinking. If we begin with God's Word and prayer, our hearts are reminded who is truly in control before anything else demands our attention.
A healthy prayer life also learns to pray with an open Bible. Too often we separate reading Scripture from prayer, but God never intended them to be disconnected. In His Word, God speaks to His people. In prayer, His people respond to Him. The two belong together. Read a passage of Scripture and allow it to shape your conversation with the Lord. When you read about His holiness, praise Him for His holiness. When you read His promises, thank Him for His faithfulness. When the Bible exposes sin, confess it honestly. When it reveals His commands, ask for the strength to obey them. Prayer becomes richer when it is guided by God's Word because we are no longer wondering what to say. We are responding to what God has already spoken.
Paul gives another practical instruction in Colossians 4:2, urging believers to "Devote yourselves to prayer with an alert mind and a thankful heart." Devotion implies consistency rather than occasional enthusiasm.
Most strong marriages are not built upon grand romantic gestures but upon thousands of ordinary conversations that deepen the relationship over time. Fellowship with God grows in much the same way. Some days our prayers will be filled with joy. Other days they will be marked by grief, confusion, or weakness. What matters is not the emotion we feel each day but the faithfulness with which we continue coming before our Father. A man who consistently meets with God will discover that prayer gradually becomes less of a discipline he forces himself to practice and more of a relationship he eagerly anticipates.
Prayer also extends beyond our personal needs. In Ephesians 6:18, immediately after describing the armor of God, Paul commands believers to "Pray in the Spirit at all times and on every occasion. Stay alert and be persistent in your prayers for all believers everywhere." Spiritual battles were never meant to be fought alone. Every Christian needs faithful brothers and sisters who pray for one another, encourage one another, and stand together in the Gospel. One of the greatest privileges God gives us is the opportunity to carry someone else's burdens before His throne. Pray for your wife before she begins her day. Pray with your children so they learn from your example that their father depends upon the Lord. Pray for your church, your pastors, your friends, your neighbors, and those who have never heard the Gospel. As our love for Christ grows, our prayers naturally become less centered on ourselves and more centered on the people God has placed in our lives.
Finally, Jesus reminds His disciples in Matthew 26:41, "Keep watch and pray, so that you will not give in to temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak." Those words remain just as relevant today. Every man faces temptations that seek to pull his heart away from Christ. No amount of self-confidence will overcome them. Victory belongs to those who recognize their weakness and continually depend upon the strength of God. Prayer keeps us spiritually awake. It reminds us that we are engaged in a real spiritual battle and that our greatest source of strength is not found within ourselves but in the Lord who has promised never to leave us.
The goal of the Christian life is not simply to become a man who prays more often. It is to become a man who walks so closely with God that prayer becomes as natural as breathing. Such a man no longer sees prayer as another responsibility to complete but as one of the greatest privileges Christ purchased through His death and resurrection. He begins each day seeking the Father's wisdom, walks through the day depending upon His strength, and ends each evening resting in His faithfulness. Over time, those daily moments of fellowship become a lifetime of knowing God, and there is no greater calling for any disciple of Jesus Christ.
Conclusion
The Greatest Privilege of Every Disciple
Prayer was never intended to be another religious duty added to an already busy life. It is one of God's greatest gifts to His children. Through Jesus Christ, the God who created the heavens and the earth has invited us into fellowship with Himself. The One who spoke the universe into existence is also the One who tells us to come boldly before His throne, not because we deserve His attention, but because His Son has made a way for us. Every prayer is a reminder that the Gospel did more than forgive our sins. It restored our relationship with our Father.
Prayer is about drawing near to the God who knows us completely and loves us perfectly. We have learned from Jesus that prayer is not built upon empty repetition but upon genuine fellowship with the Father. We have seen that biblical prayer begins with God's glory before our requests, seeks His will before our own, and trusts His wisdom even when His answers are different from what we expected. We have also seen that prayer changes the one who prays, producing peace instead of anxiety, wisdom instead of confusion, humility instead of pride, and dependence instead of self-reliance. As we remain in Christ and His Word remains in us, our prayers gradually become less focused on our own kingdom and more focused on His.
John 15:4–5, "Remain in me, and I will remain in you." Prayer is one of the primary ways we abide in Christ. Just as a branch cannot produce fruit apart from the vine, we cannot produce lasting spiritual fruit apart from daily fellowship with our Savior.
No man will ever pray perfectly. There will be seasons when distractions seem endless, when words come slowly, and when God's answers require patient waiting. Yet the hope of the Christian has never rested in the perfection of his prayers. Our hope rests in the perfection of our Savior. Jesus Christ continues to intercede for His people, and the Holy Spirit continues to help us in our weakness. Even when we struggle, God remains faithful.

title: Strongholds vs. Sins
content:
Strongholds vs. Sins
The Disciple Code
2 Corinthians 10:4–5 (NLT)“We use God's mighty weapons, not mere worldly weapons, to knock down the Devil's strongholds. With these weapons we break down every proud argument that keeps people from knowing God. With these weapons we conquer their rebellious ideas, and we teach them to obey Christ.”
John 8:31–32 (NLT)“Jesus said to the people who believed in him, "You are truly my disciples if you keep obeying my teachings. And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
Jeremiah 23:29 (NLT)“Does not my word burn like fire?" asks the LORD. "Is it not like a mighty hammer that smashes rock to pieces?”
Romans 12:2 (NLT)“Don't copy the behavior and customs of this world but let God transform you into a new person by changing the way you think. Then you will know what God wants you to do, and you will know how good and pleasing and perfect his will really is.”
A Battle Every Man Must Recognize
We use God's mighty weapons, not worldly weapons, to knock down the strongholds of human reasoning and to destroy false arguments.
STRONGHOLDS OF SIN
Breaking the Fortresses That Keep Men Bound
“We are human, but we don't wage war with human plans and methods.
We use God's mighty weapons, not mere worldly weapons, to knock down the Devil's strongholds.
With these weapons we break down every proud argument that keeps people from knowing God. With these weapons we conquer their rebellious ideas, and we teach them to obey Christ.” 2 Corinthians 10:3–5 (NLT)
Every Man Is Fighting Something
There is a battle taking place inside every man, whether he recognizes it or not. Some battles are visible to everyone around him. Others remain hidden behind a smile, a successful career, or years of church attendance. A man may appear disciplined while privately enslaved to lust. He may be respected by others while secretly consumed by bitterness. He may lead his family faithfully yet be ruled by fear, pride, or anger that no one else ever sees.
The Bible describes sin as something that grows. It deceives. It hardens the heart. Left unchallenged, it becomes a controlling influence that shapes the way a man thinks, desires, speaks, and lives.
The Bible describes these entrenched patterns as strongholds.
A stronghold is more than a recurring temptation. It is a fortress built through repeated surrender to lies instead of truth. It becomes a place where sinful thinking feels normal and obedience begins to feel difficult. What began as a single compromise eventually becomes a way of life.
Jesus Christ came to destroy the works of the devil,
“But when people keep on sinning, it shows they belong to the Devil, who has been sinning since the beginning. But the Son of God came to destroy these works of the Devil.”
(1 John 3:8),
to proclaim liberty to the captives,
"The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, for he has appointed me to preach Good News to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim that captives will be released, that the blind will see, that the downtrodden will be freed from their oppressors, (Luke 4:18),
and to set sinners free from the power of sin through His death and resurrection,
“Our old sinful selves were crucified with Christ so that sin might lose its power in our lives. We are no longer slaves to sin.
For when we died with Christ we were set free from the power of sin.
And since we died with Christ, we know we will also share his new life.
We are sure of this because Christ rose from the dead, and he will never die again. Death no longer has any power over him.
He died once to defeat sin, and now he lives for the glory of God.
So you should consider yourselves dead to sin and able to live for the glory of God through Christ Jesus.
Do not let sin control the way you live; do not give in to its lustful desires.
Do not let any part of your body become a tool of wickedness, to be used for sinning. Instead, give yourselves completely to God since you have been given new life. And use your whole body as a tool to do what is right for the glory of God.
Sin is no longer your master, for you are no longer subject to the law, which enslaves you to sin. Instead, you are free by God's grace.” (Romans 6:6–14).
Every stronghold that has been built through deception can be torn down by the truth of God's Word and the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
This is not about trying harder. It is about learning how God Himself teaches His people to fight.
What Does the Bible Mean by a Stronghold?
If you repeatedly fail against the same sin, you may be dealing with a stronghold rather than an isolated temptation.
When Paul was writing, he borrowed language familiar to the Roman world. A stronghold was a heavily fortified military fortress built to withstand attack. These structures were designed to protect what was inside and resist every attempt to overthrow them.
“We use God's mighty weapons, not mere worldly weapons, to knock down the Devil's strongholds.
With these weapons we break down every proud argument that keeps people from knowing God. With these weapons we conquer their rebellious ideas, and we teach them to obey Christ.”  2 Corinthians 10:4–5
The word strongholds is the Greek word ὀχύρωμα (ochýrōma). Awk-huyd-rom-ah, it refers to a fortress, a place of defense, or a fortified position. Paul immediately explains that these are not physical walls but arguments, proud reasoning, deceptive thoughts, and patterns of thinking that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God.
Long before a man commits adultery, he has believed lies about purity. Before greed controls his life, he has believed lies about satisfaction. Before pride dominates his heart, he has believed lies about himself. Every outward sin is first rooted in inward deception.
Satan has always worked this way from the first time in the garden, he did not begin by attacking Eve physically. He questioned God's Word.
“Now the serpent was the shrewdest of all the creatures the LORD God had made. "Really?" he asked the woman. "Did God really say you must not eat any of the fruit in the garden?" (Genesis 3:1)
The first battlefield ever recorded was in the mind.
How Strongholds Are Built
The enemy's primary weapon is deception.
Strongholds do not appear overnight. It is a progression that is both sobering and deeply practical.
“Temptation comes from the lure of our own evil desires.
These evil desires lead to evil actions, and evil actions lead to death.” (James 1:14–15)
Desire, Temptation, Sin, Death.
One compromise becomes easier to repeat than to resist. Repeated choices become habits. Habits begin shaping desires. Those desires slowly reshape the mind until what once troubled the conscience begins to feel ordinary.
“Be careful then, dear brothers and sisters. Make sure that your own hearts are not evil and unbelieving, turning you away from the living God.
You must warn each other every day, as long as it is called "today," so that none of you will be deceived by sin and hardened against God.” (Hebrews 3:12–13)
Sin is deceitful because it never presents its true destination.
Pornography promises satisfaction while producing slavery.
Pride promises strength while destroying humility.
Bitterness promises justice while poisoning the soul.
Greed promises security while leaving the heart empty.
Fear promises protection while stealing obedience.
Every stronghold begins with believing that something other than God will satisfy us more than obedience to Him.
That is the oldest lie in history.
The Strongholds That Commonly Enslave Men
The enemy does not need every man to struggle with the same temptation. He only needs each man to become mastered by something other than Christ.
“You may say, "I am allowed to do anything." But I reply, "Not everything is good for you." And even though "I am allowed to do anything," I must not become a slave to anything.”
(1 Corinthians 6:12)
A stronghold asks one simple question:
What has become your master?
For one man, it is pornography hidden behind late-night screens.
For another, it is anger that erupts whenever his authority is questioned.
For another, it is success that has quietly become an idol.
Some men live for approval. Others live for comfort. Others cannot imagine a day without alcohol, gambling, endless entertainment, social media, or constant distraction. Some appear disciplined on the outside while secretly nourishing resentment that has lived in their hearts for years.
Whatever continually rules your thoughts, shapes your decisions, and competes with your love for Christ deserves honest examination.
Jesus said,
"No one can serve two masters. For you will hate one and love the other, or be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.” (Matthew 6:24)
The question is not whether you worship, but rather whom—or what—you worship.
The Lies Behind Every Stronghold
Every fortress stands on a foundation.
If every spiritual fortress is built upon a lie, we convince ourselves that:
"I'll stop tomorrow." "No one will know." "I deserve this." "This isn't hurting anyone."
"This is just who I am." "God could never forgive me." "My past defines me."
“For you are the children of your father the Devil, and you love to do the evil things he does. He was a murderer from the beginning and has always hated the truth. There is no truth in him. When he lies, it is consistent with his character; for he is a liar and the father of lies.” (John 8:44).
His strategy has always been deception. He does not create truth. He twists it.
We cannot overcome lies by stronger emotions or greater willpower.
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered every temptation with words,
Matthew 4:4 “But Jesus told him, "No! The Scriptures say, 'People need more than bread for their life; they must feed on every word of God.'"
4:7 “Jesus responded, "The Scriptures also say, 'Do not test the Lord your God.'"
4:10 "Get out of here, Satan," Jesus told him. "For the Scriptures say, 'You must worship the Lord your God; serve only him.'"
The sword Christ used is the same sword He has placed into the hands of His people—the Word of God.
“Put on salvation as your helmet, and take the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” (Ephesians 6:17).
Christ Has Already Won the Decisive Victory
Freedom comes through truth, not willpower.
A stronghold may feel permanent, but the cross declares otherwise.
" Our old sinful selves were crucified with Christ so that sin might lose its power in our lives. We are no longer slaves to sin." (Romans 6:6)
The believer does not fight for just any victory.
He fights from Christ's victory.
Jesus did not merely forgive sin. He broke its dominion.
That does not mean temptation disappears. It means sin is no longer the rightful master of those who belong to Christ.
“So if the Son sets you free, you will indeed be free.” (John 8:36)
Freedom is not found in self-confidence.
Freedom is found in our one and only Savior, Jesus Christ.
Pulling Down Strongholds
Discipleship is one of God's primary tools for breaking strongholds.
God has not left His people without weapons.
He calls us to confess our sins honestly,
“But if we confess our sins to him, he is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from every wrong.” (1 John 1:9),
repent continually,
“Now turn from your sins and turn to God, so you can be cleansed of your sins.” (Acts 3:19),
renew our minds through His Word,
“Don't copy the behavior and customs of this world, but let God transform you into a new person by changing the way you think. Then you will know what God wants you to do, and you will know how good and pleasing and perfect his will really is.” (Romans 12:2),
walk by the Spirit,
“So I advise you to live according to your new life in the Holy Spirit. Then you won't be doing what your sinful nature craves.” (Galatians 5:16),
pray without ceasing,
“Keep on praying.” (1 Thessalonians 5:17),
encourage one another daily
“You must warn each other every day, as long as it is called "today," so that none of you will be deceived by sin and hardened against God.” (Hebrews 3:13),
and put sin to death rather than negotiate with it
“So put to death the sinful, earthly things lurking within you. Have nothing to do with sexual sin, impurity, lust, and shameful desires. Don't be greedy for the good things of this life, for that is idolatry.” (Colossians 3:5).
Scripture never tells us to make peace with sin. It tells us to crucify it.
Strongholds fall when lies are replaced with truth, when hidden sin is brought into the light, when pride gives way to humility, and when a man learns that obedience is not the enemy of joy but the pathway to it.
The Christian life is not perfection achieved in a day. It is daily surrender to Christ, trusting His grace, relying on His Spirit, and refusing to return to the chains from which He has delivered us.
Disciple Challenge
Men must fight for themselves and their families, spiritually.
Spend time alone with God and answer these questions honestly.
What sin have I begun to tolerate instead of fight?
What lie about God or myself have I believed?
What has mastered my thoughts more than Christ?
What secret habit would I be ashamed for my wife, children, or closest brothers in Christ to know?
Am I feeding the flesh while expecting to grow spiritually?
Is there someone I need to confess to or seek accountability from today?
If Jesus searched every hidden corner of my life, what fortress would He lovingly call me to surrender?
Do not answer these questions quickly. Open your Bible. Pray honestly. Ask the Holy Spirit to search your heart, just as David prayed:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my thoughts.
Point out anything in me that offends you, and lead me along the path of everlasting life." (Psalm 139:23–24)
The strongest man is not the one who has never struggled. The strongest man is the one who continually humbles himself before Christ, refuses to make peace with sin, and keeps walking in the light of God's truth. The battle against strongholds is ultimately not about proving your strength.
